summary: The article examines whether modern pilgrimage retains spiritual sanctity or has become commercialized tourism. It covers economic impact, social-media-shaped pilgrimage tales, the loss of the journey itself, and environmental damage at sacred sites. It closes with efforts toward sustainable pilgrimage and a call for personal reflection on authenticity.
one_line: A critical look at how commercialization, tourism, social media and environmental strain challenge the authenticity of modern pilgrimage and sacred places.
key_facts: Pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place as an act of spiritual devotion, found in the Islamic Hajj to Mecca, Hindu Char Dham Yatra, Christian Camino de Santiago, and the Buddhist path to Mount Kailash.

On October 15th, 2023, John Smith, a professor of Comparative Religion at Global University, argued that pilgrimage routes are crowded with shops, hotels and branded signage, diluting the search for enlightenment.
In 2023, over 25 million people reportedly participated in the Kumbh Mela in India, and towns like Varanasi saw revenues surge.
Lourdes in France and Vatican City remain thriving because of their religious significance.
Anthropologist Jane Doe, who visited Lourdes in September 2023, questioned whether sacred sites with their own merchandise lines are commodifying belief itself.
David Wilson, who completed his pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in November 2023, said the journey felt performed and that there is pressure to have a monumental spiritual awakening.
Religious studies scholar Sophia Khan argued that flying in and staying at a luxury hotel bypasses the journey meant to prepare pilgrims for the destination.
Mount Kailash, revered in both Buddhism and Hinduism, is threatened by pilgrim influx; environmental activist Luo Wang says pilgrims leave garbage that contradicts their reverence.

Michael Thompson, who managed a hostel on the Camino trail, observed that many who start as tourists find deeper, more introspective thoughts along the way and that it is not for others to judge who is a pilgrim.
Several organizations now promote sustainable pilgrimage practices, including eco-friendly travel and support for local communities.
Emily Redding, head of one such initiative, says the aim is balancing respect for traditions with modern pilgrims' needs and that a sacred journey isn't simply another holiday.
The article concludes that sacred places and pilgrimage tales remain core cultural heritage, but introspection is needed to discern personal truth amid commodification.
